articles.author: Jen Sherman
articles.content: The US has more big chains but in Australia produce is better quality – and bread doesn’t taste like cake I poked. I pulled. I looked in confusion at the head of garlic I was holding, wondering why the cloves weren’t coming apart. When I dug my nails in and finally broke out a clove, its skin was pierced and there were scratch marks in the flesh. It had only been a few weeks since I moved back to Australia from the US, after a 10-year stint in San Diego; only a few weeks since I cooked with garlic cloves. Surely I hadn’t lost finger strength that quickly? Turns out, it wasn’t me. It was the garlic. Since that first Australian head of garlic, I’ve discovered that Australian garlic is tighter than the US variety. Over there, a few gentle rubs prise the cloves apart. Here, you’ve really got to put some effort in – I suspect that’s why you can buy a packet of garlic cloves in supermarkets and I never saw such a product in the States. Garlic in Australia is more expensive, too. Continue reading...

articles.content: Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast The government will save more than it spends, says Jim Chalmers , but it won’t be a “slash and burn” budget update. Unlike the federal budget, where we get plenty of notice of when it will be handed down, the government only gives us a few days notice for the mid-financial year economic and fiscal outlook (or Myefo). There’s still a fair bit of work to do to finalise it all, but we’ve made enough progress to be confident that at this stage there will be a modest net save in the budget. We’re not going to slash and burn in the budget where that would impact the payments that people receive or where it would impact some of the more sensitive parts of the economy. But we haven’t focused the savings on just one portfolio. There will be a number of savings in the mid-year update. They will be substantial, as I said. These are serious times. You can see in the quite extraordinary reaction on the stock market just how volatile global markets are right now. I think it’s a bit of a symbol of the quite extraordinary volatility, unpredictability that we’re seeing play out in markets in the AI sector, but more broadly as well. Continue reading...

articles.content: We must compete with each other. But in these straitened times, a sense of justice and collegiality has never been more important At this lectern last year, Kerry O’Brien struck home when he warned of the erosion of media freedom. Of Israel’s killing of our colleagues in Gaza and beyond. Of Trump’s endorsement of Saudi Arabia, so soon after its dismemberment of a Washington Post writer. Of the prosecution, here in Australia, of tax office whistleblower Richard Boyle. I won’t dare to attempt anything so eloquent and urgent, though I do want to reflect for a moment on what I think might be the larger threat to the press in Australia right now. And that’s the humble bean counter. Continue reading...

articles.content: Despite the highest wage growth in years, we wait for signs of workers getting ahead of inflation – or of the supposed benefits of the AI boom Get our daily political email , free app or daily news podcast It’s rare of late to get good economic news, but on Wednesday the wage figures from the Bureau of Statistics showed a nice bump in wages . Private-sector wages rose 1.0% in the September quarter for an annual growth of 3.4%, the highest in two years. But even with these good numbers, real wages went backwards, showing just how tough things are for workers. Each year the September quarter is the big time for a wage increase. This isn’t because your boss is feeling romantic and likes to remember when “grass was green and grain was yellow” . No, it’s because it is the first quarter of the new financial year and also the quarter where workers on the minimum/award wage get a pay rise via the Fair Work Commission: Continue reading...

articles.author: Nils Pratley
articles.content: The Claude AI developer’s unique setup is supposedly high-minded, but still represents extraordinary power concentration Boardroom governance matters, even in the world of big tech, it turns out. The business of how companies are run, investors are discovering, can be more complicated than handing the founder or superstar chief executive as much control as he wants (it’s usually a he) and waiting for brilliant returns to appear. Sometimes a few checks on power are useful, especially when a crisis strikes. This revelation is no revelation at all, of course. For about 30 years until the first generation of big US tech companies came along, the thrust of corporate governance thinking was to insist on the basic fairness of the principle of “one share, one vote”. The owners should be able to chuck out misbehaving or underperforming managers by a simple majority, in other words. Continue reading...

articles.content: The role AI played in job losses at Australia’s NAB, Qantas, Canva and Atlassian is far from clear – but it may prove to have more impact on the stock market than the jobs market Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast In 1987, the Nobel prize winning economist Robert Solow remarked: “You can see the computer age everywhere but in the productivity statistics.” At the time, computers had been around for 40 years. Real productivity gains did emerge in the 1990s after the arrival of the internet, but they were short-lived. Four years after the launch of ChatGPT, the pattern seems to be much the same: lots of hype and excitement but with very little productivity growth. The main economic impacts, as in the 1990s dotcom era, have been a stock market boom and huge investment in infrastructure (fibre optics then, datacentres today), betting on future demand that has yet to emerge. Continue reading...

articles.author: Kat George
articles.content: The practice you’ve noticed is colloquially known as ‘review gating’, writes consumer affairs and policy professional Kat George . And no, it isn’t legal Read more Australian customer service questions I have noticed that when I get an email inviting me to review a product or service I have purchased online or physically, if I select a high rating I am taken to Google to write a review. However, if I select a low rating, I am then told “We are sorry” etc and asked what is wrong. I am not taken to Google to write a review. This would lead to very biased reviews. Is this practice legal? – Tom, Queensland Kat says: Screening reviews and sorting feedback based on a consumer’s initial sentiment is known colloquially online as “review gating” . It’s a dark pattern that is common enough that Google has banned it outright. And while the Australian consumer law doesn’t name the practice explicitly, it is clearly prohibited under laws relating to business reviews and false and misleading practices. Continue reading...
